analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover as long a hospital stay as the attending physician deems medically necessary.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required group and individual health insurance, Medicare and Medicaid managed care plans, Medigap policies, and several federal health programs to cover a hospital stay as long as the attending doctor, consulting with the patient, judged medically appropriate. Insurers could not require the doctor to get the plan's permission before prescribing a length of stay, and could not pay providers to discharge patients early. It was introduced by Senator Dianne Feinstein with Republican Senator Olympia Snowe as cosponsor and was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where no further action was taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients facing surgery, childbirth recovery, or serious illness who would otherwise face pressure from their insurance plan to leave the hospital before they and their doctor felt ready.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans, individual market coverage, Medicare and Medicaid managed care plans, and Medigap policies to cover whatever hospital length of stay the attending physician, in consultation with the patient, determines is medically appropriate [S2][S3].

Prohibits plans from requiring providers to obtain prior authorization from the insurer for a prescribed length of stay, and from offering providers money or incentives to induce early discharge or shorter stays [S3].

Bars plans from penalizing or reducing reimbursement for providers who follow the standard, and from limiting cost-sharing within a covered stay to be more burdensome than the earlier part of the stay [S3].

Extends the same protections to the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, military and veterans' care, the Children's Health Insurance Program, Indian Health Service, and Peace Corps coverage [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care plans, which would cover longer stays and lose the pre-authorization lever; employers and premium-payers may absorb some of the cost through premiums.

drawbacks.text: Plans may still impose deductibles and coinsurance on the covered stay, so patients bear some added cost-sharing as stays lengthen [S3].

By allowing the attending provider rather than the plan to determine the stay length, the bill removes an insurer cost-control tool, which in the general working of health insurance tends to raise premiums; supporters accept that trade as the price of protecting patients.
The bill sets no minimum number of days for any procedure; it relies entirely on the attending provider's judgment, so protection varies case by case [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete for patients: a doctor, not an insurer's authorization clerk, decides when a patient is ready to leave the hospital. The cost is higher premiums and the loss of a tool insurers use to limit spending. The bill tries to limit abuse by allowing plans to negotiate reimbursement levels and keep cost-sharing rules, but it leaves the fundamental trade — more coverage, higher premiums — unresolved.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on January 20, 1999, with Senator Olympia Snowe as its one cosponsor, giving it a bipartisan sponsor pair [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on January 20, 1999 [S1][S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill during the 106th Congress, and it received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and HMOs, which kept their authority to require pre-authorization for hospital stays and to press providers toward shorter stays. Patients gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on January 20, 1999.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Health insurers and HMOs
against.role: Industry whose utilization-review practices the bill targeted
against.what_they_did: During this era the industry publicly opposed federal mandates restricting insurers' ability to manage hospital stays, as part of its broader campaign against the patients' bill of rights.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat introduced the bill and its only cosponsor was a Republican, so it had support from both parties at introduction; no votes were ever held, so party positions beyond sponsorship were never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would bar plans from requiring prior authorization for hospital lengths of stay and from paying providers to discharge patients early [S3], removing tools insurers used to keep hospital costs down. Longer covered stays raise insurer costs, which is why insurers resisted such mandates.

Coverage for medically appropriate stays means more hospital revenue for longer admissions, and doctors rather than insurers would control discharge timing. Patients and hospitals were on the same side of this line.
The bill applies to self-insured plans [S3], so employers would face higher expected claim costs, offset partly by the value of healthier, more secure employees.
